content: Azithromycin is associated with the risk of QT interval prolongation, particularly in cases of overdose or when used in patients with concurrent illnesses or medications that cause electrolyte imbalances or prolong the QT interval. Close monitoring is recommended when azithromycin is co-administered with drugs such as quinidine, azithromycin, quinine, quizartinib, ranolazine, ribociclib, rifabutin, rifampin, rilpivirine, rimegepant, riociguat, risperidone, ritonavir, rivaroxaban, romidepsin, ruxolitinib, selpercatinib, sertraline, sevoflurane, simvastatin, siponimod, sodium bicarbonate, sodium citrate, sodium picosulfate, solifenacin, sorafenib, sotalol, sulfamethoxazole, sunitinib, tacrolimus, talazoparib, telavancin, temocillin, tetrabenazine, thiamine, thioridazine, thiothixene, tobramycin, tolvaptan, topotecan, toremifene, trazodone, trifluoperazine, trimethoprim, trimipramine, triptorelin, tropisetron, typhoid vaccine (live), umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol, valbenazine, vandetanib, vardenafil, vemurafenib, venetoclax, venlafaxine, verapamil, vilanterol/fluticasone furoate, voclosporin, voriconazole, vorinostat, warfarin, and ziprasidone. These interactions may increase toxicity, alter drug levels, or exacerbate QT prolongation, necessitating dose adjustments, alternative therapies, or enhanced monitoring. Azithromycin has been associated with elevated liver enzymes (ALT, AST), creatinine, LDH, and bilirubin, as well as gastrointestinal symptoms such as dyspepsia, flatulence, mucositis, oral moniliasis, gastritis, vomiting, diarrhea, and pseudomembranous colitis. Other reported adverse effects include headache, somnolence, bronchospasm, taste disturbances, leukopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Rare but serious reactions include arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular tachycardia, torsades de pointes), cardiovascular death, anaphylaxis, hepatic necrosis, hepatic failure, and severe skin reactions (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis). Azithromycin may also exacerbate symptoms of myasthenia gravis or induce a myasthenic syndrome. Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) has been reported in neonates, and parents should be advised to monitor for vomiting or feeding irritability. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) is a potential complication, ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected, discontinue unnecessary antibiotics and initiate appropriate treatment. Azithromycin is present in human milk, but no serious adverse effects have been reported in breastfed infants. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for azithromycin and potential risks to the infant. Available data in pregnant women have not identified any drug-associated risks for major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Azithromycin is used to treat bacterial infections, including eye infections when formulated as an ophthalmic solution. It is ineffective against non-bacterial infections. Proper administration techniques, such as shaking the dropper and avoiding contamination, are essential. Temporary eye irritation, stinging, or blurred vision may occur. Prolonged or repeated use may lead to secondary infections, including fungal infections. Patients should be informed about potential drug interactions, which may alter the efficacy or safety of azithromycin. Overdose can be harmful, and emergency medical attention should be sought if serious symptoms occur. Proper storage and disposal of the medication are necessary to maintain its efficacy and prevent misuse. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about azithromycin. Patients should consult their healthcare provider for personalized medical advice and complete information about their specific health needs.
